analysis.one_liner: Tightens Pentagon rules requiring defense contractors to open their books and justify prices.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it harder for defense contractors to charge the Pentagon inflated prices. It would require companies bidding on sole-source or cost-reimbursement contracts to hand over real cost data, narrow the loophole that lets companies label their products 'commercial items' to skip price scrutiny, require large defense contractors to disclose their sales prices, profit margins, and pricing strategies publicly each year, and reward contractors with faster payments when they cooperate with Pentagon cost reviews. The bill never received a hearing or a vote in the House.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, whose money funds the roughly $800 billion defense budget, would benefit if the Pentagon could see contractors' actual costs and margins before agreeing to prices. Service members and the public would get the same weapons at prices supported by real data, and the bill's public disclosure provisions would let journalists and watchdogs see contractor profit margins for the first time.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Truth in Negotiations Act so that companies expected to be the only bidder, or bidding on any cost-reimbursement contract, must submit certified cost or pricing data rather than escaping the requirement [S2].

It narrows the 'commercial item' exemption, which currently lets companies sell products to the Pentagon at prices without the cost scrutiny that applies to other contracts, by requiring that commercial pricing be based on genuine competition with at least two viable competing offers and comparable sales volumes [S2].

It would require large traditional defense contractors to report annually to the Defense Department — and the Department to publish — the percentage change in their sales prices, their gross margins by product category, how much of their revenue growth came from price increases versus volume, and a detailed narrative explaining their pricing strategy, including any case where prices rose faster than costs [S2].

It creates a pilot program tying accelerated progress payments to a contractor's responsiveness to Pentagon requests for cost and pricing information, with traditional contractors eligible for up to 95 percent payment rates only if they provide certified cost data within 30 days of a request [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Defense contractors — the large traditional contractors whose sole-source and cost-reimbursement contracts would face certified cost data requirements, narrower commercial exemptions, annual margin disclosure, and payment incentives tied to cooperation — would bear the cost of providing data and could face pressure on the margins they earn from Pentagon contracts.

drawbacks.text: Critics of expanded cost-data and disclosure requirements on defense contracting argue that heavier pre-award paperwork slows procurement and deters companies from bidding, which matters when the Pentagon needs to rapidly ramp up production of munitions and shipbuilding [S2].

The disclosure mandate in Section 5 applies to traditional contractors regardless of contract size, so even smaller traditional defense suppliers would face annual reporting on margins and pricing strategy, a compliance cost an honest supporter would acknowledge [S2].

The progress-payment pilot rewards contractors with faster cash — up to 95 percent payment rates — in exchange for cooperation, meaning the bill would route additional government cash flow to compliant contractors rather than penalizing uncooperative ones [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is real: the Pentagon buys most major weapons systems without genuine competition, and studies of price gouging and inflated pricing on sole-source contracts have repeatedly drawn attention to large contractor margins. The bill's mechanisms — real cost data before negotiation, honest labeling of what is actually 'commercial,' and public margin disclosure — target the specific structures that let those prices stand. The main costs are compliance paperwork and possible slowdowns in bidding, which defenders of streamlined acquisition raise in good faith; the disclosure requirement could have been limited to the largest contractors. On balance the benefits for taxpayers plausibly outweigh the compliance burden, though the bill would have needed refinement in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Armed Services and Oversight committees on the day it was introduced, and neither committee ever reported it, so it never came up for a House vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Garamendi, joined by Rep. Chris Deluzio, introduced the bill on June 30, 2023, and it was referred the same day to the House Armed Services Committee and the House Committee on Oversight and Accountability [S1].
Three House Democrats cosponsored the bill [S3].

After referral, the only further action was the sponsor's introductory remarks published in the Congressional Record on July 6, 2023; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action is recorded for the remainder of the Congress [S4].
The bill expired on January 3, 2025, when the 118th Congress ended, without a vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large defense contractors are better off: they avoid the certified cost-data requirements, the narrowed commercial-item exemption, and the annual public disclosure of gross margins and pricing strategy that the bill would have imposed. Taxpayers continue to pay negotiated prices on sole-source contracts without this additional visibility into contractor costs and profits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large defense contractors kept current pricing terms

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so the record shows no opposition; all recorded support came from Democrats (the sponsor, the co-introducer, and 3 Democratic cosponsors), and the Republican-controlled committees to which it was referred never acted on it [S3][S4].

industries.industry: Traditional defense contractors (e.g., major weapons and systems makers on sole-source and cost-reimbursement contracts)
industries.note: The bill would require them to certify cost data on contracts where they currently escape it, would narrow the 'commercial item' exemption many use to avoid price scrutiny, and would force annual public disclosure of gross margins and pricing strategy. Their interest in blocking the bill ran against taxpayers', since the bill's whole purpose was to expose and curb prices that exceed actual costs.

industries.industry: Defense subcontractors in traditional contractor supply chains
industries.note: The bill's definitions reach contractors performing subcontracts under cost accounting standards coverage, so suppliers below the prime would face the same cost-data and disclosure demands. The compliance burden would fall on smaller firms even though the pricing problem is largest at the top.
